findings: The prompt lets cuts split a phrase from a following dependent clause or clausal complement (subordinating/relative/‘that’–type clauses), underestimating how much meaning and entailment are lost when the clause is separated.

diagnosis.why: The inserted fallback to keep a marker together with a following dependent/clausal complement shifted the model's top-ranked cut choices (depth‑1 improved slightly but depth‑2 worsened notably), so the edit mainly changed the first one or two preferred cuts. That behavior helped examples where an adverbial or clause was kept with its head, but it also caused cuts to move into noun phrases, enumerations, and multiword names (e.g. splitting 'Cirque du Soleil' or 'assistance of 80 police'), producing balanced wins and losses and largest harm in the ≤5 bin.
diagnosis.lesson: Limit the fallback to true subordinating/clausal markers and avoid applying it when the 'marker' is part of an NP, named entity, or enumeration, because this change mainly alters top-ranked choices and will hurt short/medium-latency settings if it forces cuts inside multiword noun phrases.

changelog: Delete C4: it largely restates C3 (clausal material supplying predicate/argument/scope) and encourages attention to noun-phrase internal boundaries; removing this redundant rule reduces rule competition that can push cuts into multiword names/NPs (the critique and history show clausal-attachment rules can force cuts inside NPs and named entities).
findings: The prompt allows cuts inside multiword proper names or titles, treating internal boundaries as acceptable splits and so fragmenting named entities.
The prompt cuts immediately after fronted temporal/adverbial phrases, detaching them from their governing verb and producing incoherent or misleading early pieces.

When forced to choose between two imperfect internal cuts, the prompt prefers cuts that break verb–object adjacency; instead it should prefer cuts that avoid separating a verb from its core object/complement.
